name: GAIN: food fortification, nutritious food markets, workforce nutrition and food-systems policy (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: almost all of the result is the fortification branch, which GAIN reports only as a world total (1.55 billion people); split over its fortification countries with weight on the most populous (India, Nigeria, Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Ethiopia), a judgment, as GAIN publishes no country split.
summary: GAIN, a Geneva foundation, spent 61.6 million dollars on programmes in its year to June 2025: helping governments and food companies fortify salt, flour, oil and rice (1.55 billion people reached, by its own count), building markets and small businesses for nutritious food in Africa and Asia, workplace nutrition, and food-systems planning and policy. We estimate about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, almost all from fortification: children's later earnings from iodized salt and less anaemia from iron-fortified food. The biggest uncertainty is how much of the yearly benefit of long-running national fortification programmes depends on GAIN's support (we credit GAIN with about a tenth of the resources, and a quarter of the benefit as depending on support), and everything but the anaemia effect, which comes from evaluations of real fortification programmes, is discounted for missing data. The dollar is a past average (a year's spending over what it reached, not a price per item), so the result is scaled by our figure for GAIN's next dollar. With every judgment this uncertain, the result is mostly uncertainty: from a few hundredths to several years per 1,000 dollars.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN)

resources.title: Keats et al. 2019, large-scale fortification in low- and middle-income countries (meta-analysis)
GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators 2019, health effects of dietary risks

rows.label: Programme expenses (direct project and personnel costs)
rows.explainer: Total expenses less fundraising and administration: GAIN's direct project costs (37,998,908 dollars) and personnel costs (23,588,849 dollars) together, 61,587,757 dollars, the programme spending in GAIN's charity record.

rows.label: Gifts in kind (partners' contributions to the Global Diet Quality Project)

source.title: GAIN, audited financial statements, year to 30 June 2025 (PricewaterhouseCoopers SA)

rows.explainer: In-kind contributions from partners, booked as both income and expense (note 12): not GAIN's own money, so they leave the cost here (Convention 2); they fund the evidence work in the policy branch, whose attribution share already counts partners.

rows.label: Programme spending of GAIN's own money
rows.explainer: Programme expenses less partners' in-kind contributions.

rows.label: Share of programme spending on food fortification (including salt iodization, the Premix Facility, biofortification and supplements)
rows.explainer: GAIN publishes no spending by programme. Anchors: the Gates Foundation, whose GAIN grants are mostly large-scale fortification, spent 8.9 of 62.1 million dollars of restricted funds (14%, note 8); Germany (5.7 million) funds biofortification and fortification among other work; food fortification took 27% of sub-awards (note 11). 25%, from 15% to 40%.

rows.label: Share on nutritious food value chains and enterprises (markets, small businesses, the N3F fund)
rows.explainer: The Netherlands' market-based diet-quality programme (value chains for vegetables and animal-source foods, vendors, food markets) spent 26.6 of 62.1 million dollars of restricted funds (43%, note 8), with the EU, SDC, Irish Aid and Norway funding similar work. 45%, from 35% to 55%.

rows.label: Share on workforce nutrition
rows.explainer: A small team advising companies and the Workforce Nutrition Alliance (about 100 workplaces in the year); no donor in note 8 funds it on a large scale. 3%, from 1% to 6%.

rows.label: Share on policy, food-systems planning, evidence and influencing
rows.explainer: The rest: food-systems pathways and planning tools, policy and advocacy (Nutrition for Growth, climate and nutrition), data, evaluations and publications. GAIN says 22% of its projects mainly influence policy and about 18% generate evidence (annual report p. 3), consistent with about a quarter of spending.

rows.explainer: Spreads fundraising and administration over the programmes in proportion to their cost; partners' in-kind contributions are out of both sides.

People reached by fortified foods GAIN supported, 2024/25

source.title: GAIN's 2024/25 results, on its GuideStar profile (from the 2024-2025 annual report)

rows.explainer: GAIN's own count of people reached in the year through the large-scale fortification and biofortification programmes it supports (88.6 million of them through its Premix Facility). It is a yearly flow (people eating fortified foods this year), but a count of the populations covered by national programmes, not an independent coverage survey: GAIN's annual report (p. 7) says an audit was undertaken to review and assess its methods for estimating the numbers reached. Delivery is in ff_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Low-income consumers targeted by GAIN's value-chain projects

source.title: GAIN, Annual Report 2024-2025
source.quote: GAIN's interventions to strengthen value chains to improve availability and consumption of nutritious and safe foods target a population of at least 9 million low-income consumers across Mozambique, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

rows.explainer: GAIN's own figure for the consumers its value-chain projects target, not a count of buyers reached; reaching them is in vc_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Consumers reached by the businesses the N3F fund lent to

source.title: GAIN, Annual Report 2024-2025
source.quote: logistics, reaching at least 3 million consumers.

rows.explainer: The Nutritious Foods Financing Facility (N3F), which GAIN set up and invests in, lent 7.6 million dollars to 13 small food businesses whose products reach at least 3 million consumers (annual report p. 3).

rows.label: Consumers in the value-chain branch
Workers reached by workforce nutrition programmes

source.title: GAIN, Annual Report 2024-2025
source.quote: In 2024/25, GAIN contributed to healthier diets of 572,237 workers through the adoption of workforce nutrition programmes supported by GAIN

rows.explainer: Workers at about 100 workplaces whose employers adopted programmes (canteen food, nutrition education, health checks, breastfeeding support) with GAIN's technical help or through the Workforce Nutrition Alliance.

rows.label: People in countries whose food-systems plans GAIN helped draft and adopt in the year
rows.explainer: GAIN supported the drafting, validation and approval of food-systems action plans, strategies and road maps in Mozambique, Nigeria, Benin, Kenya and Ethiopia (annual report p. 3), about 450 million people together (World Bank population figures, 2024: Nigeria about 230, Ethiopia about 130, Kenya about 56, Mozambique about 35 and Benin about 14 million), with smaller policy work elsewhere (Indonesia's front-of-pack labelling rule, Rwanda's agriculture strategy). A judgment because how many people a plan touches is unclear: 300 to 600 million.

rows.label: People reached in the year (all branches)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the branches reach people in very different ways, so this sum is not a count of people helped.

rows.label: Cost per person reached
rows.explainer: Context only; dominated by the fortification reach.

rows.label: Years of protection one year's work gives
rows.explainer: Every branch counts one year's flow against one year's spending (Convention 3): fortified food eaten in the year, consumers and workers reached in the year. The policy branch counts its own years through the won-reform rows.

rows.label: Healthy years lost to dietary risks worldwide, 2017

source.title: GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators, Health effects of dietary risks in 195 countries, 1990-2017, Lancet 2019;393:1958-72
source.quote: In 2017, 11 million (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 10-12) deaths and 255 million (234-274) DALYs were attributable to dietary risk factors.

rows.explainer: The burden of poor diets (too little fruit, vegetables, whole grains, legumes; too much sodium and processed meat), the outcome GAIN's diet-quality work tries to move. The uncertainty interval is the range.

rows.label: World population, 2017

source.title: UN DESA, World Population Prospects: the 2017 revision (press release, 21 June 2017)
source.quote: The current world population of 7.6 billion is expected to reach 8.6 billion in 2030

rows.explainer: To turn the global burden into healthy years lost per person per year.

rows.label: Healthy years lost to poor diet per person per year
rows.explainer: The world average, about 0.034 a year. The people GAIN's market and workplace work reaches are younger and poorer, with less of the heart disease that dominates this burden: that is in each branch's external validity.

rows.label: Share of the people reached whose fortified foods include iron
rows.explainer: GAIN's count mixes salt (iodine only), edible oil (vitamins A and D), wheat and maize flour and rice (iron, folic acid, zinc) and biofortified crops; it gives no split by food. Half, from 30% to 70%: flour and rice programmes in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Nigeria and Ethiopia are among GAIN's largest, and salt programmes cover more people than any other food. GAIN's figure counts people, not people times foods, so one person can eat both iodized salt and iron-fortified flour: the iron and iodine shares overlap and can add to more than 1.

rows.label: Healthy years lost to dietary iron deficiency per person per year (India, 2017)
rows.explainer: The site's figure for the burden iron fortification addresses (IHME GBD 2017, India, all ages, both sexes, as GiveWell uses it for iron fortification), about 0.0086 healthy years per person per year. India is among GAIN's largest fortification countries; South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa have similar burdens. Only illness is counted: GBD counts no deaths from iron deficiency.

rows.label: Fall in anaemia with large-scale food fortification

source.title: Keats et al. 2019, Improved micronutrient status and health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries following large-scale fortification, Am J Clin Nutr 109:1696-1708

rows.explainer: The meta-analysis of real-world fortification programmes in low- and middle-income countries (not efficacy trials), mostly before-and-after and comparison-group studies; the 95% CI is the range. Applied to the burden of iron deficiency, so it counts no anaemia from other causes.

rows.label: Healthy years of illness averted per person reached, iron
Share of the people reached who get iodized salt through programmes GAIN supports
rows.explainer: GAIN has run universal salt iodization programmes in 17 countries (its charity record) and still supports national salt programmes; salt is the most widely fortified food. 60%, from 40% to 80%, a judgment as GAIN gives no split by food.

rows.label: Share of the population under 15 in GAIN's fortification countries
rows.explainer: Children whose development iodine affects. About a quarter of India's and Indonesia's people are under 15, over 40% in Nigeria and Ethiopia (World Bank, population ages 0-14); 32%, weighted towards Asia where most of the reach is, from 25% to 43% (GiveWell's Sub-Saharan figure).

rows.label: Years of childhood over which iodine acts
rows.explainer: Anchored on GiveWell's salt iodization model (Iodine!B17, 15 years by definition), the full benefit spread over 15 years of childhood. Children under 15 over these 15 years (0.32 ÷ 15 = 2.1% a year) is about the yearly births per person in GAIN's countries, weighted towards Asia, so each year of iodized salt protects about one year's births in pregnancy and infancy, when iodine matters most (the IQ gap below is in children up to five). The range is ours.

rows.label: IQ points lower in iodine-deficient children than in iodine-replete ones (meta-analysis)
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (@iodine.iq_points_deficient_vs_replete: 7.5 points, 5 to 10), from a meta-analysis of trials and cohorts in children up to five, mostly in moderate to severe deficiency; the milder deficiency of GAIN's countries is the next row.

rows.label: IQ loss iodized salt prevents in GAIN's countries, relative to the meta-analysis's

source.title: GiveWell, salt iodization cost-effectiveness analysis (Parameters, row 55)

rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on GiveWell's salt iodization model: a quarter of a standard deviation (about 4 IQ points) where deficiency is mild to moderate, its reading of the randomised trials (Zimmermann et al. 2006, Gordon et al. 2009 average 0.24), 0.18 to 0.36 SD in its low and high cases. Against the meta-analysis's 7.5 points (0.5 SD) that is half, from 0.35 to 0.7.

rows.label: Share of the IQ gain that lasts into adulthood
rows.explainer: The trials followed children for one to two years; GiveWell allows 20% for fade-out (0.8, from 0.4 to 1), and we use its figure.

rows.label: Yearly gain in ln(earnings) in adulthood per person reached, from iodine
rows.formula: ff_iodine_share * ff_share_under15 / ff_childhood_years * ff_iq_points_deficient * ff_severity_vs_meta * @givewell_shared.wage_gain_per_iq_point * ff_lasting_share
rows.explainer: Per person-year of iodized salt: the children's share of the people reached, a fifteenth of the full childhood benefit, the IQ points kept at the site's one wage gain per IQ point (GiveWell's 0.67%), less fade-out.

rows.label: Years from childhood exposure until the earnings gain starts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for iodine (@iodine.years_until_income_benefits_iodine: 15 years, 12 to 20): the gain from protecting a child in pregnancy and infancy starts when that child starts work.

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for how long a long-term income gain lasts (GiveWell's working years, 40), read by every model that counts one (INV-13).

rows.label: Discounted lifetime gain in ln(earnings) per person reached
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate, the wait included.

rows.label: Household sharing of an earner's gain
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (GiveWell's): an earner's income gain is shared with the household.

rows.label: Share of a consumer's diet-related health loss removed in a year of better access to nutritious foods
rows.explainer: GAIN's value-chain projects make vegetables, eggs, fish and dairy more available and safer in local markets (12,000 trained vegetable vendors in Kenya, rebuilt markets in Mozambique) with media campaigns; midline assessments in Kenya and Mozambique show better vendor performance and access (annual report p. 8) but no measured change in consumers' diets or health. A consumer buying slightly more vegetables or animal-source food removes a small share of the diet burden: 0.3%, from 0.05% to 1%, a judgment with no direct anchor.

rows.label: Healthy years averted per consumer per year, value chains
Share of a worker's diet-related health loss removed in a year of a workplace nutrition programme
rows.explainer: Workplace programmes change the food served at work (often one main meal a day), add nutrition education and health checks; reviews find modest gains in fruit and vegetable intake. 1%, from 0.2% to 3%: a larger share than market work because the meal itself changes, a judgment.

rows.label: Healthy years averted per worker per year, workforce nutrition
Share of the diet-related health loss a food-systems plan removes per person per year once carried out
rows.explainer: National food-systems plans set priorities and budgets across agriculture, trade, social protection and health; carried out, they can shift a country's diet only slowly and partly. 0.05% of the burden per person per year, from 0.01% to 0.3%, a judgment.

rows.label: Chance the plans are carried out enough to change diets
rows.explainer: Many national nutrition and food-systems plans go underfunded; one in five, from 5% to 40%, a judgment.

rows.label: Years from a plan's approval to its effect on diets
rows.explainer: Plans approved in 2024/25 need budgets and programmes before diets change; two years, from one to four.

rows.label: Years a plan counts, discounted
rows.explainer: A won policy counts the site's years for a won reform (How impact is counted), the wait until it takes effect discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Healthy years averted per person covered, policy and planning
Deaths per person-year the programmes can reduce
rows.explainer: 0: GBD counts no deaths from iron or iodine deficiency, and the fortification meta-analysis pools no mortality outcome; the deaths from neural tube defects that folic acid prevents are in other_unmodelled_share. Diet-quality work averts deaths too, but its burden in DALYs already counts them.

rows.label: Relative fall in those deaths
rows.explainer: 0, as above.

rows.label: Indirect deaths per direct death averted
rows.explainer: 0: no deaths are counted directly.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached
Share of deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: Unused: the model counts no deaths directly, so the age split doesn't change the result.

rows.label: Share aged 5-14 of those over five
rows.explainer: Unused: the model counts no deaths directly, so the age split doesn't change the result.

rows.label: Share aged 15-49 of those over 15
rows.explainer: Unused: the model counts no deaths directly, so the age split doesn't change the result.

rows.label: Illness averted as a share of deaths' and income's value
rows.explainer: 0: illness (anaemia, diet-related disease) is counted directly in healthy years through the bridge, not as a share.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per person reached
rows.explainer: 0 here: the stillbirths iodine prevents in deficient mothers are in other_unmodelled_share.

rows.label: Healthy years of illness averted per person reached (all branches)
rows.formula: (ff_people * ff_dalys_per_person + vc_people * vc_dalys_per_person + wf_people * wf_dalys_per_person + pol_people * pol_dalys_per_person) / people_reached
rows.explainer: For reading only: each branch's healthy years averted, over everyone reached.

rows.label: Internal validity of the fortification evidence
rows.explainer: The anaemia effect comes from before-and-after and comparison studies of programmes, which can mistake other trends (deworming, rising incomes) for fortification; the IQ effect from small randomised trials of iodine. 0.7, from 0.5 to 0.9, below GiveWell's 0.8 for its iodine trials because most of the anaemia evidence is not randomised.

rows.label: External validity, fortification
rows.explainer: Only how far effects measured when programmes were new carry to the established programmes GAIN mostly supports today (the burden, the shares of people by food and the count are their own rows): as programmes mature, mills and salt producers are better at fortifying but intakes from other sources rise. 0.8, from 0.6 to 0.95, a judgment.

rows.label: Share of the year's fortification benefit that depends on the support programmes keep getting
rows.explainer: Most of the 1.55 billion people would keep eating fortified food without this year's support: the laws, mills' equipment and premix supply are in place. Programmes do slip without monitoring, premix credit and technical help (salt iodization has reverted where support stopped, GiveWell notes). A quarter, from 10% to 50%, a judgment.

rows.label: Food companies' cost of fortifying, per person reached per year

source.title: Horton, Mannar and Wesley 2008, Micronutrient fortification (iron and salt iodization), Copenhagen Consensus best practice paper
source.quote: approximately $0.05/person/year for iodine and $0.12/person/year for iron fortification of wheat and maize flour

rows.explainer: What salt producers and millers spend on the fortificant, equipment and processing: 5 cents for iodized salt, 12 cents for iron-fortified flour; 8 cents for GAIN's mix of foods, the two as the range.

rows.label: Other organisations' and governments' resources for the same programmes, relative to GAIN's
rows.explainer: No published accounting splits national fortification programmes' resources among the organisations that support them, so there is no reference class. Governments regulate and monitor, and other international and national organisations support many of the same programmes: together about as much as GAIN, from half to twice.

rows.label: GAIN's share of the resources behind the fortification programmes
rows.explainer: GAIN's fortification spending over everyone's: its own, the other organisations' and governments', and food companies' cost of fortifying for the 1.55 billion people (about 120 million dollars), about a tenth.

rows.label: Share of the people counted who eat adequately fortified food
rows.explainer: GAIN's count is of populations covered by the programmes; not all buy the fortified brands, and much food is under-fortified. The meta-analysis's effects are already of real programmes with their usual shortfalls, so only GAIN's counting is at issue here: 75%, from 50% to 100%.

rows.label: Missing-data step, fortification: the iodine earnings term
rows.explainer: Thin for iodine: the IQ effect is from trials of iodine supplements and the earnings from studies of IQ and wages, not from evaluations of salt programmes like GAIN's, so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12). The canonical average reads this row for the fortification branch.

rows.label: Missing-data step, fortification: the anaemia term
rows.explainer: Measured: GAIN counts the people its fortification programmes reach (an audit reviewed its estimation methods), and the effect on anaemia is from the meta-analysis of real large-scale fortification programmes in low- and middle-income countries (Keats et al. 2019), delivered the same way; doubts about the count are in ff_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Evidence, value chains
rows.explainer: The diet burden is a world average dominated by heart disease in older adults; GAIN's consumers are younger and poorer, and part of the burden comes from too much sodium and processed food that market work doesn't touch. 0.6, from 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Share of the diet change that wouldn't happen anyway, value chains
rows.explainer: Markets develop anyway as incomes rise; vendors trained might have improved without GAIN. 60%, from 30% to 90%.

rows.label: GAIN's share of resources, value chains
rows.explainer: The businesses, vendors and N3F's other investors put in their own money and time: half, from 30% to 80%.

rows.label: Share of the targeted consumers actually reached
rows.explainer: 9 million is a target population, not a count of buyers; half, from 20% to 80%.

rows.label: Share of the branch's consumers actually reached
rows.explainer: The targeted consumers at the reached share; the N3F firms' consumers are already a count of people reached.

rows.label: Missing-data step, value chains
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured change in diets or health; the effect is a judgment.

rows.label: Evidence, workforce nutrition
rows.explainer: As for value chains: a world-average diet burden applied to workers, who are working-age adults in middle-income and low-income countries. 0.6, from 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Share that wouldn't happen anyway, workforce
rows.explainer: Many of the companies (often large exporters and multinationals) have their own health programmes; half the change, from 30% to 80%, is due to the programmes GAIN helped start.

rows.label: GAIN's share of resources, workforce
rows.explainer: The employers pay for the food and the programmes; GAIN gives technical help. A quarter, from 10% to 50%.

rows.label: Missing-data step, workforce
rows.explainer: Thin: workers covered are counted, but no change in diets or health is measured.

rows.label: Evidence, policy and planning
rows.explainer: As for value chains, the world-average diet burden applied to younger, poorer populations. 0.6, from 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Share of the plans that wouldn't exist, or would be worse, without GAIN
rows.explainer: Governments draft these plans under the UN Food Systems Summit process with many partners; GAIN's tools and staff help. 30%, from 10% to 60%.

rows.label: GAIN's share of resources behind the plans
rows.explainer: Governments' own staff, FAO, GIZ, the World Bank and others work on the same plans: 15%, from 5% to 30%.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used: GAIN's share of resources behind the plans
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Missing-data step, policy
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured outcome of the plans.

rows.label: Funging and leverage
rows.explainer: GAIN's money is almost all restricted donor grants for set projects (note 8); an unrestricted gift mostly keeps teams and country offices running between grants, so it neither displaces nor pulls in much other money. 1, from 0.9 to 1.05.

rows.label: Cash and cash equivalents, 30 June 2025

source.title: GAIN, audited financial statements, year to 30 June 2025 (PricewaterhouseCoopers SA)

rows.explainer: What GAIN held in cash at the year end.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Cash at the year end over a year's spending, about two months.

rows.label: Years from spending to the benefit
rows.explainer: Technical assistance, premix and vendor training take some months to show in what people eat: half a year, from a quarter to a full year.

rows.label: Middle of the year of benefit
Discount for the waits
rows.explainer: Every wait is discounted at the shared rate; the policy branch's own wait is in pol_years_counted, and the income gain's from delivery.

rows.label: Evidence, fortification
Adjustments common to both fortification terms
rows.formula: ff_evidence_adj * ff_counterfactual_adj * ff_attribution_share * ff_implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount

rows.label: All adjustments, fortification: the iodine earnings term
All adjustments, fortification: the anaemia term
All adjustments, value chains
rows.formula: vc_evidence_adj * vc_counterfactual_adj * vc_attribution_share * vc_reach_share * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * vc_missing_data_adj

rows.label: All adjustments, workforce
rows.formula: wf_evidence_adj * wf_counterfactual_adj * wf_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * wf_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Discount for the wait before a gift is spent, policy
rows.explainer: The gift waits in GAIN's cash before it is spent, as in the other branches; the wait from a plan's approval to its effect is in pol_years_counted.

rows.label: All adjustments, policy
rows.formula: pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj * pol_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * pol_gift_wait * pol_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Internal validity (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_internal_validity + vc_spend * 1 + wf_spend * 1 + pol_spend * 1) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only. The other branches' doubts are in their evidence_adj.

rows.label: External validity (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_external_validity + vc_spend * vc_evidence_adj + wf_spend * wf_evidence_adj + pol_spend * pol_evidence_adj) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Evidence (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_evidence_adj + vc_spend * vc_evidence_adj + wf_spend * wf_evidence_adj + pol_spend * pol_evidence_adj) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Counterfactual (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_counterfactual_adj + vc_spend * vc_counterfactual_adj + wf_spend * wf_counterfactual_adj + pol_spend * pol_counterfactual_adj) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: GAIN's share of resources (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_attribution_share + vc_spend * vc_attribution_share + wf_spend * wf_attribution_share + pol_spend * pol_attribution_share_shared) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: GAIN's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_attribution_share + vc_spend * vc_attribution_share + wf_spend * wf_attribution_share + pol_spend * pol_attribution_share) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' used shares, for reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.label: Implementation (average)
rows.formula: (ff_spend * ff_implementation_adj + vc_spend * vc_reach_share + wf_spend * 1 + pol_spend * 1) / (ff_spend + vc_spend + wf_spend + pol_spend)
rows.explainer: Spending-weighted average of the branches, for reading only.

rows.label: Missing-data step (average)

rows.label: Treatment costs averted
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for prevention programmes: anaemia and diet-related illness prevented saves its treatment.

rows.label: Rebound effects
rows.explainer: 0: rebound immunity applies to malaria prevention only.

rows.label: Investment of income increases
rows.explainer: The site's figure for programmes with long-term income gains (here iodine's).

rows.label: Effects not modelled, net, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits not in the chain: neural tube defects (folic acid in flour cuts their odds by 41%, Keats et al. 2019), deaths and stillbirths among them and from iodine deficiency in pregnancy, vitamin A deficiency (fortification protects nearly 3 million children a year from it, same review), goitre (odds down 74%), multiple micronutrient tablets for pregnant women in Bangladesh (75 million tablets, annual report p. 7), and the incomes of vendors, farmers and small businesses GAIN supports. Harms and risks: excess iodine where salt is over-iodized, nutrition-labelled processed foods drawing buyers from fresher ones, funds spent on projects that close early (the year's restructuring after donor cuts). Net +15%, from -5% to +40%, a judgment.

rows.label: Supplementary shares on the health terms
rows.explainer: Treatment costs averted apply to illness prevented (anaemia, diet-related disease), with the net unmodelled effects.

rows.label: Supplementary shares on the earnings term
rows.explainer: Investment of income applies to the iodine earnings gain only, with the net unmodelled effects; no treatment is averted by a higher IQ.

rows.formula: (uov_income * unmodelled_income_adj + (uov_deaths + uov_stillbirths + uov_from_daly) * unmodelled_health_adj) / (uov_income + uov_deaths + uov_stillbirths + uov_from_daly)
rows.explainer: Each term's own supplementary shares, weighted by the term's value: the earnings gain takes investment of income, the health terms treatment costs averted, both the net unmodelled effects.
